item.title: Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought
item.description:
Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in the second quarter of 2026, more than the national statistic agency CBS’s initial assessment.

The CBS said higher export volumes and stronger household spending were the main reasons for the revision. The second, more detailed assessment is published around 85 days after the end of the quarter.

Over the 12-month period GDP grew by 1.6%, its fastest rate since the first quarter of 2025. That figure was also revised upwards from an initial 1.3%.

The labour market improved, with an additional 15,000 employees and registered freelancers in the second quarter. The initial assessment said the total number of jobs had dropped by 8,000.

item.title: Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
item.description:
Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.

The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.

The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.

The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.

France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.

The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.

Goals downgraded

The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.

Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.

But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”

Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.

“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.

A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

item.title: Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab
item.description:
Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prosecutors have demanded a seven-year jail sentence for a man who blew up a drugs lab in Rotterdam, causing a blast that killed three people and damaged neighbouring flats.

Jalal O., 37, was renting the garage store on Schammenkamp to produce cocaine when it exploded on the evening of January 29, 2024. One of the victims was his 22-year-old cousin, who was working in the lab at the time.

A forensic investigation found that the blast was caused by vats of acetone, used in the production of the drug, catching fire at the back of the building. A neighbouring block of flats was so badly damaged that five homes had to be demolished.

Prosecutors said O. had “allowed financial gain to prevail over the safety of local residents and others”. They said he had sublet the property via a “shady arrangement”.

O. helped with the search for missing neighbours immediately after the disaster, but was arrested a few days later. He told the district court in Rotterdam he found the events “terrible”, but denied that he was using the garage for drug production.

Prosecutors produces messages between O. and his cousin showing steam rising from barrels of acetone, while residents complained of the chemical smells from the building. The prosecution said the defendant’s denials were “totally unbelievable”.

One woman who was evacuated from one of the flats said the explosion had had a devastating effect on her health.

“I have lost part of my hearing, my hair has fallen out and I have lost my teeth through stress,” she said. “I have flashbacks and sleep badly. I have nightmares in which I fall into the fire and burn to death.”

item.title: AP says sharing images from Meta glasses is not allowed
item.description:
AP says sharing images from Meta glasses is not allowed

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned on Tuesday that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“You may not simply share, publish, or use for other purposes photos and videos in which other people are recognisably depicted,” the Dutch Data Protection Authority said in a statement.

“People must be able to walk the streets freely without having to fear that someone is filming them without their knowledge and subsequently sharing the images or posting them on the internet,” board member Katja Mur said.

The group also warned against using the glasses in sensitive locations, like hospitals, courthouses, and religious buildings. It advises those organisations to ban use of the glasses on their premises.

Last month, the consumer watchdog Consumentenbond issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

item.title: Which Dutch city actually fits your budget and lifestyle in 2026
item.description:
Partner content

Which Dutch city actually fits your budget and lifestyle in 2026

September 22, 2026

Moving to the Netherlands means picking not just a country but also a city, and in 2026 that choice matters more than it used to. Rents in the unregulated sector rose 7.3% nationally over the past year, according to the latest Pararius Huurmonitor, pushing the average to roughly €21 per square metre. But that average hides a lot of variation. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, and Eindhoven, the so-called G5, each behave quite differently right now, and the gap between them is worth understanding before you commit to a lease.

Here’s how the five compare.

Amsterdam is still the most expensive place to rent in the country by a wide margin, at €28.53 per square metre after a further 5.1% rise this year. That premium buys you the strongest job market for tech, finance, and creative roles, plus the density of international life that draws people here in the first place. An 80m² apartment typically runs €2,300 to €2,500 a month before utilities. If your work is anchored in the city, it’s worth starting your search among the apartments in Amsterdam currently listed.

Rotterdam had one of the sharpest price increases of any G5 city this year, up 10.4% to €22.78 per square metre, and it’s still noticeably cheaper than Amsterdam for comparable space. The city’s pull comes from its modern skyline, its logistics and maritime industry, and an international business culture that doesn’t feel like a smaller copy of the capital. You’ll generally get more square metres for your budget here. Current listings for apartments in Rotterdam are a reasonable place to gauge what that looks like in practice.

The Hague rose 6.5% in price this year to €22.42 per square metre and remains a common choice for people working at the international courts, embassies, or corporate headquarters based there. It has a slower pace than Rotterdam or Amsterdam, more green space, and the coastline is a short cycle away. Neighbourhoods range from the stately Statenkwartier to livelier, more central pockets, so it’s worth browsing a spread of apartments in The Hague before narrowing down an area.

Utrecht climbed 5.9% to €21.61 per square metre and sits at the literal centre of the country’s rail network, which matters more than it might sound. The city has the Netherlands’ largest university, a well-preserved medieval core, and a train commute of 30 minutes or less to nearly any other major Dutch city. That combination of culture and connectivity keeps competition for listings tight. Have a look through apartments in Utrecht to see what’s currently on the market.

Eindhoven posted the second-largest increase in the G5 this year, up 10.0% to €19.55 per square metre, still the most affordable of the five despite that jump. The city runs on ASML, Philips, and a wider “Brainport” ecosystem of tech and engineering firms, which explains why it draws a heavily specialised international workforce. If that’s your field, apartments in Eindhoven are where to start looking.

What this means for your search: In a market this tight, landlords generally expect a gross income of three to four times the monthly rent, and they’ll want to see it upfront. Have your employment contract, recent payslips, and a short summary of your rental history ready before you start applying, since properties in demand can be gone within days. Pararius only lists properties from verified, professional agents, which at least removes one layer of risk from an already competitive process. You can view all listings here.

item.title: Low earners offered €6,000 subsidy to buy used electric cars
item.description:
Low earners offered €6,000 subsidy to buy used electric cars

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Low and middle income households will be able to claim up to €6,000 from the government towards the cost of buying a second-hand electric car, three years after the last subsidy was abolished.

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said the government wanted to make EVs more accessible. Figures published last month showed that only 2% of electric cars and plug-in hybrids were bought by the lowest 10% of wage earners.

People with a pre-tax income of up to €27,533 will be eligible for €6,000 towards the cost of a second-hand electric car, while those earning less than €35,793 will be able to claim €4,000 – provided that they scrap their old fossil-fuel car with a registered dealer.

The amount is intended to reflect the difference in price between second-hand electric vehicles relative to petrol and diesel cars.

A total of €52.4 mln has been made available to fund the scheme, which the cabinet hopes to have up and running by the start of next year following an online consultation.

“It is very important for this cabinet that people with modest means can make the switch to an electric car and enjoy the benefits,” Bertram said.

Falling sales

The government scrapped the last scheme to subsidise purchases of new and used electric vehicles in 2024. Discounts on road tax for electric and hybrid vehicles were also phased out.

In the following year EV sales dropped from 32% of the total market to 26%, with the most popular model, the Tesla Model Y, slumping from 2,000 sales in November 2023 to less than 500 in January 2024.

CBS figures showed that people on the lowest incomes were most likely to buy diesel cars and two-thirds of those in the bottom 20% bought vehicles that were more than 10 years old.

item.title: Dancing bananas are back as social media site Hyves relaunches
item.description:
Dancing bananas are back as social media site Hyves relaunches

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Once the biggest social network in the Netherlands, Hyves has come back online after 13 years.

The “gezelligste platform” in the Netherlands has been relaunched by owners Mediahuis, which hopes to tap into nostalgia and distrust of American social media companies.

First launched by a group of Dutch friends in 2004 who wanted to share photos, Hyves hit its peak in 2010 with 10 million users, more than half of the country’s population.

The same year it was acquired by Mediahuis Netherlands, which also owns the newspapers De Telegraaf and NRC

Users soon began to abandon the site to a new social networking site, Facebook, and by 2013, the site was offline. The games section of the website lived on as Hyves Games.

“Hyves wants to do things differently,” Mediahuis said in a statement. The group promises to keep users’ data within Europe and will not use algorithms to determine what content people see.

The site’s infamous dancing banana will also return.

New accounts will be limited to 10,000 on the first day and 5,000 every day after. Mediahuis hopes to have 1.5 million users by the end of the year.

item.title: Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid
item.description:
Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch man whose 14-year-old son died after he was denied medical treatment for Covid-19 has been jailed for 23 years by a court in Belgium.

Rennlhy Manuela covered up the death of his son, Jairon, for eight weeks, refusing to let his siblings enter his bedroom and telling his mother he was out of the house when she tried to visit him.

Manuela, who belonged to a strict Pentecostal sect, refused to consult a doctor when Jairon fell ill at the end of 2021, instead relying on paracetamol, a liquid diet and prayers for his recovery.

The court of justice in Antwerp said Manuela “made his child’s life subordinate to his radical religious convictions”. He was convicted of murder by a jury and sentenced to 23 years in prison, three years more than prosecutors demanded.

The boy died in the night of January 3 and 4 after falling in the bath. When police were called to the house, they found his body underneath a blanket in an advanced state of decay, with traces of ketamine in his blood.

Manuela and his adult housemates had hoped God would answer their prayers to bring Jairon back to life.

Mother raised alarm

Jairon’s mother, Danica, raised the alarm after she contacted the boy’s school across the Dutch border in Tilburg, only to be told he had been signed out months earlier.

She had been denied access to the villa in Turnhout, where Manuela lived with his children and several other members of the religious community.

Four other adults were given sentences of between one and three years in the case. The jury said Manuela had caused “irreperable suffering” by “preventing [Jairon’s] mother and brothers saying goodbye in a humane manner”.

item.title: One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS
item.description:
One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Water companies have called for PFAS chemicals to be banned in pesticides after a study showed that one-third of people are exposed to high levels of the “forever chemicals” in drinking water.

An analysis by Greenpeace of every postcode in the Netherlands showed that the water in 32% of areas contains PFAS levels that are at least 1.5 times the recommended safe level.

The environmental inspection agency ILT blames the increased use of trifluoroacetic acid in pesticides by agricultural sectors such as potato farming, which has almost doubled in the last two years. The ILT says two tonnes of the chemical end up in the water supply per year.

The highest concentrations are in the provinces of Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland, with towns such as Zaandam, Purmerend and IJmuiden recording 14.3 nanograms per litre.

PFAS is a collective label for thousands of highly stable chemical compounds that are used extensively in packaging, liquid chemicals and products such as waterproof clothing and non-stick cooking pans.

They are attractive to industry because they are extremely durable, but prolonged exposure increases the risk of cancer, immune system problems, low fertility and damage to unborn babies.

High blood levels

A recent study by the public health agency RIVM showed almost everyone in the Netherlands has unhealthy levels of PFAS in their blood.

Greenpeace compiled a dataset and built an online tool allowing householders to see how much PFAS is in their drinking water, with a map to show the most polluted and least polluted areas.

“We think this information should be available to everyone, so we asked a data analyst to set out clearly how much pollution is in the water per location,” campaign leader Eline Bosman told NRC.

There are strong regional variations, with the northern provinces of Drenthe, Friesland and Groningen showing almost no PFAS chemicals in drinking water.

Patricia van der Linden of Vewin, the association of Dutch drinking water suppliers, said the west of the country drew its water supply from rivers and reservoirs, which are more polluted than water sources in rural areas.

“Ground water contains less pollution than surface water,” she said. “In places where we use surface water for drinking water, we have to take more steps to purify the water.”

Immune system

Although none of the water supplies exceed the legal limit set by the European Union, they are well above the RIVM’s advisory limit of 4.4 nanograms.

The agency lowered the guideline level in 2023 in the light of new information that showed PFAS chemicals have a greater impact on the immune system than previously thought.

Germany, the Netherlands and the Scandinavian nations have been lobbying since February 2023 for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides throughout the EU.

RIVM spokesman Coen Berends told NRC: “We can see that banning individual types of PFAS makes a difference, but really the whole group should be banned.”

item.title: Student who made Hitler salute at TU Eindhoven has left NL
item.description:
Student who made Hitler salute at TU Eindhoven has left NL

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The public prosecution service has said it will not investigate an incident involving a Hitler salute during a lecture at TU Eindhoven after the student voluntarily left the country.

According to the university, a during a first year calculus class, the student made racist remarks in the packed lecture hall and performed a Nazi salute. Fellow students intervened, resulting in a fight.

The university executive board said in a statement that the behaviour was “unacceptable” and it was investigating.

The student was later arrested on suspicion of threatening behaviour, but prosecutors dropped the case because he was deemed to be “vulnerable”.

Following talks with the student and his father, the youth, who turned 18 this month, choose to leave the Netherlands, the public prosecution service said. They would not disclose his country of origin.
